questions.title: Why is hyperspherical energy (HE) a good proxy for preserving semantic generation ability?
questions.question_body: The paper uses hyperspherical energy (HE) defined as HE(W) = \(\sum_{i\neq j} \|\hat{w}_i-\hat{w}_j\|^{-1}\) with \(\hat{w}_i=w_i/\|w_i\|\). I am confused why this quantity should correlate with semantic generation ability of a pretrained diffusion model. Can someone provide an intuitive explanation or empirical justification for why preserving HE preserves semantics, as opposed to, say, preserving Euclidean distance between weight matrices?

questions.title: How exactly does an orthogonal matrix preserve pairwise neuron angles?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that applying the same orthogonal transformation \(R\) to all neurons preserves pairwise hyperspherical similarity (angles). Can someone show a short mathematical derivation that for normalized neurons \(\hat{w}_i\), \(\langle R\hat{w}_i, R\hat{w}_j\rangle = \langle\hat{w}_i,\hat{w}_j\rangle\)? Also, does this hold for non-normalized neurons?

questions.title: Why is Cayley parameterization chosen to enforce orthogonality and what are its limitations?
questions.question_body: Section 3.3 uses the Cayley transform \(R=(I+Q)(I-Q)^{-1}\) with skew-symmetric \(Q\) to parameterize orthogonal matrices. Why is Cayley preferred over e.g. QR or exponential map? The paper mentions Cayley only produces matrices with determinant \(+1\). What practical consequences does this det=+1 constraint have for finetuning, and could we miss useful reflections (det=-1)?

questions.title: How do you compute gradients through the Cayley transform efficiently?
questions.question_body: The Cayley transform includes an inverse \((I-Q)^{-1}\). During training we must backpropagate through this matrix inverse. How is this done practically (naive inverse + autograd, Woodbury/Neumann approximations, custom solver)? Are there stability or speed issues for large block sizes?

questions.title: What does block-diagonal parameterization of \(R\) mean for convolutional layers?
questions.question_body: The paper suggests using a block-diagonal \(R=\mathrm{diag}(R_1,\dots,R_r)\) and claims it has an interpretation for convolutional layers, e.g. when number of blocks equals input channels. Could someone clarify concretely: if a conv kernel has shape \(C_{out}\times C_{in}\times k\times k\), how is \(R\) applied and what does each block operate on? Does blocking across channels restrict mixing between channels?

questions.title: How do OFT and LoRA compare algebraically — are they equivalent updates under some conditions?
questions.question_body: The paper rewrites OFT as \(W^0+(R-I)W^0\) and says the term \((R-I)W^0\) is analogous to LoRA's low-rank additive update. Under what conditions (e.g. low-rank \(R-I\) and full-rank \(W^0\)) do OFT and LoRA become similar? Can OFT represent arbitrary LoRA updates or vice versa?

questions.title: How is the COFT constraint \(\|R-I\|\le \epsilon\) enforced in practice given Cayley parameterization?
questions.question_body: COFT requires \(\|R-I\|\le\epsilon\). The paper approximates \(R\approx I+2Q+O(Q^2)\) and enforces a constraint on \(Q\) instead. Which matrix norm is used for the constraint (operator norm, Frobenius)? How is projection implemented (clipping singular values, scaling)? How is \(\epsilon'\) mapped to \(\epsilon\) in practice?

questions.title: When using the Neumann series approximation \(R\approx I+2Q+O(Q^2)\), when does the series converge?
questions.question_body: The paper assumes the Neumann series for \((I-Q)^{-1}\) converges in operator norm. For what spectral radius of \(Q\) does the series converge? Is there an empirical or theoretical guideline to keep \(\|Q\|<1\)? What happens if \(\|Q\|\ge 1\) during training?

questions.title: Is HE(W) well-defined if two normalized neurons become identical (zero denominator)?
questions.question_body: HE uses terms \(\|\hat{w}_i-\hat{w}_j\|^{-1}\). If during training two neurons align exactly, that difference becomes zero and the term blows up. How is this handled numerically? Do they regularize or cap the inverse distances? Does orthogonality avoid this issue?

questions.title: How are OFT parameters allocated for Transformer attention layers in Stable Diffusion?
questions.question_body: The experiments say OFT was applied to the same layers where LoRA is used (typically attention). Which matrices in cross-attention / self-attention were transformed with \(R\) exactly (query/key/value/proj_out)? Were the transforms applied to weight shapes like \(d\times d\) or different? Any implementation details would help.

questions.title: How is block size \(r\) chosen and how does it affect expressivity vs parameter cost?
questions.question_body: Block-diagonal \(R\) reduces parameters by factor \(r\). Is there a recommended rule-of-thumb for choosing \(r\) relative to dimension \(d\)? How does increasing \(r\) (smaller blocks) change the model's ability to represent useful rotations and the empirical finetuning performance?

questions.title: Why does re-scaled OFT add a diagonal scaling \(D\) and how does that preserve HE?
questions.question_body: Re-scaled OFT uses \(z=(R W^0 D)^\top x\) with diagonal \(D=\mathrm{diag}(s_i)\). The paper says re-scaling neurons does not change HE because HE uses normalized neurons. But if we change magnitudes and then later normalize for HE, could interactions with layernorms / activations alter downstream behavior? Any caveats about learning positive \(s_i\) only?

questions.title: How is the positivity constraint on diagonal \(D\) enforced during training?
questions.question_body: In re-scaled OFT, they require diagonal elements \(s_i>0\). How is this implemented? Do they parametrize \(s_i=\exp(t_i)\) or use ReLU + epsilon? Are there stability concerns if some \(s_i\) become very large or very small?

questions.title: Does OFT affect normalization layers (LayerNorm/BatchNorm) or only linear weights?
questions.question_body: The paper focuses on applying OFT to weight matrices (fully connected/attention/convs). In modern diffusion models there are many LayerNorms. Should OFT be applied to normalization parameters as well? Could rotating neuron directions interact poorly with learned scale/shifts of LayerNorm?

questions.title: What is the computational training overhead of OFT compared to LoRA and full finetuning?
questions.question_body: Although OFT introduces fewer parameters than LoRA in some regimes, Cayley transform and matrix inverses seem expensive. Practically, for a standard finetuning run on Stable Diffusion v1.5, how does wall-clock training time and GPU memory for OFT compare to LoRA and full finetuning?

questions.title: How robust is OFT to different initialization and learning rates?
questions.question_body: The method initializes \(R=I\) (via \(Q=0\)). Does OFT require very small learning rates similar to standard finetuning, or can it tolerate larger steps? Are there stability issues if updates push \(R\) far from identity quickly?

questions.title: Why does OFT empirically converge faster than LoRA or other adapters?
questions.question_body: The paper hypothesizes two reasons: changing neuron directions is effective, and optimization on a smooth hypersphere manifold helps. Can someone provide a more concrete optimization perspective: does parameterizing via orthogonal matrices reduce ill-conditioning, or does it impose implicit preconditioning that accelerates convergence?

questions.title: How exactly is the control consistency metric computed for C2I, S2I, and L2F?
questions.question_body: The paper introduces a control consistency metric: estimate control from generated image and compare to original. For C2I they use IoU and F1, for S2I mean IoU and accuracy, and for L2F mean \(\ell_2\) between landmarks. How are control signals predicted (which off-the-shelf models), and are these metrics computed per-image or averaged over dataset splits?

questions.title: Can multiple orthogonal matrices from different tasks be composed to yield a multi-task model?
questions.question_body: The conclusion mentions compositionality: orthogonal matrices from multiple OFT finetuning tasks can be multiplied together to remain orthogonal. If we have \(R_a\) (task A) and \(R_b\) (task B), is \(R_b R_a W^0\) expected to perform both tasks, or do interactions break task-specific adaptations? Any theoretical intuition or empirical results?

questions.title: What norm is used for the COFT constraint \(\|R-I\|\le\epsilon\) and why choose that norm?
questions.question_body: The paper writes \(\|R-I\|\le\epsilon\) but does not specify whether this is operator (spectral) norm, Frobenius norm, or elementwise. Which norm is used in experiments, and how does the choice affect the set of allowed orthogonal matrices (e.g. it's qualitatively different whether spectral vs Frobenius)?

questions.title: How sensitive are results to the block-sharing option where \(R_i=R_j\) for all blocks?
questions.question_body: The block-diagonal parameterization allows sharing the same block across positions to reduce parameters further. Did the authors test shared vs independent blocks? How does sharing affect expressivity and empirical performance in subject-driven and controllable tasks?

questions.title: Is the HE objective in Eq. (1) actually optimized during training or only implicitly enforced via orthogonality?
questions.question_body: Equation (1) states minimizing the HE difference, but then the practical method learns an orthogonal \(R\) which guarantees HE preservation. Do they ever add HE as an explicit regularizer during training, or is HE preservation only achieved by constraining the update to orthogonal transforms?

questions.title: How are edge cases handled when Cayley denominator \((I-Q)\) becomes near-singular?
questions.question_body: If \(I-Q\) is close to singular, the Cayley transform will be numerically unstable. Is there any mechanism (e.g. regularization on \(Q\), clamping eigenvalues) to prevent singularity? Did the authors observe such instabilities during training?

questions.title: Why does minimizing HE (as in Liu et al. 2021) hurt pretrained semantic structure, while OFT preserves it?
questions.question_body: The paper contrasts OFT (preserve HE) with orthogonal over-parameterized training that minimizes HE for classification (which helps generalization). Intuitively, why would minimizing HE destroy pretrained semantic structures in generative diffusion models, whereas preserving HE is better?

questions.title: How is the projection of \(Q\) onto \(\|Q\|\le\epsilon'\) implemented during projected SGD?
questions.question_body: The paper says the constraint on \(Q\) can be enforced via projected gradient descent. Do they project by scaling the Frobenius norm, clipping singular values, or truncating entries? Which projection was used in experiments and why?

questions.title: How does OFT interact with textual conditioning and cross-attention weights specifically?
questions.question_body: In diffusion models like Stable Diffusion, cross-attention mixes image latents and text embeddings. If OFT rotates attention weight matrices, could that disrupt alignment between spatial features and text embeddings? How is semantic alignment preserved when applying a layer-shared orthogonal rotation to attention weights?
